source.title: On Implications of Scaling Laws on Feature Superposition

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a theoretical argument that superposition and feature universality cannot both be complete accounts under its scaling-law assumptions, so it calls for qualifying the superposition account. It does not empirically test neuron polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The paper's Model A/Model B comparison is a hypothetical argument based on assumptions, not a reported measurement or experiment on trained models. Its cited empirical and interpretability findings are from other work and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A theoretical note that argues the superposition account, as a complete theory of feature representation, conflicts with feature universality under Kaplan scaling-law aspect-ratio invariance. That is a specific argument that V3's mechanism needs restating. It contains no measurements of neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author argues that superposition as a complete theory and feature universality cannot both hold, given scaling-law invariance to aspect ratio. Computational capacity scales with parameters, while representational capacity scales with total neurons. The author offers no resolution and speculates about compression schemes beyond superposition and superlinear cross-layer superposition.
record.recipe_differences: No intervention or measurement recipe is applied; the argument is a theoretical comparison of hypothetical transformer shapes.
record.method_sensitivity: The argument depends on the assumed aspect-ratio change at fixed parameter count and comparable performance.
record.problems: The reasoning depends on assumptions that equal-performing models learn the same features and that feature sparsity is determined by the data. The text describes its cylinder analogy as non-rigorous and reports no empirical test of the argument.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the Model A/Model B comparison is hypothetical and its quantities are derived from assumptions rather than reported measurements on trained models. Cited findings, including those about dictionary-learning features, are results from other work.

untested.parts: No language-model MLP neurons or their token/context responses measured.
No empirical test that superposition causes polysemantic neurons. The argument is purely derived from assumptions (equal-loss models learn the same features; sparsity fixed by data).
Initialization, regularization and noise are not examined.
No polysemantic-neuron share or architecture comparison is measured. Aspect ratio appears only hypothetically.
No measurement choices are compared. The remark that low activations of dictionary features look polysemantic is cited from Bricken et al.

record.verdict_notes: There are no rows, and that is appropriate: the paper reports no measurements. The V3 label rests only on a theoretical argument with strong assumptions, which the author partly calls non-rigorous (the cylinder analogy). Researchers should weight it lightly. The paper targets superposition as a theory of features, not directly as the cause of neuron polysemanticity. It is a single-author preprint.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier neurons or mixed visual inputs are examined.
No language-model MLP neurons or token/context responses are measured.
The paper reasons about implications of superposition under feature universality, but does not measure polysemantic neurons or establish that superposition causes them.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not examined as causes.
No polysemantic-neuron share, activation-function comparison, or performance cost is measured.
No canonical polysemantic neurons or their input features are reinterpreted.
No neuron measurement or explanation-scoring choices are compared.

relationships.condition: Hypothetical transformers of equal parameter count and loss but different aspect ratios (Model B: 2x width, 1/4 layers), assuming feature universality
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows (none exist). Model B has half the neurons, so it needs twice the features per neuron and sparser features. Sparsity is fixed by the data, so superposition as a complete account or universality must be revised. This is a non-empirical argument.
relationships.display_finding: The wider, shallower model has half the neurons, so it would need twice the features per neuron and sparser features. Since sparsity is fixed by the data, either superposition as a complete account or universality must be revised; the argument is not empirical.

relation.reason: The note's own argument bears on whether V3's mechanism holds as stated. The rules count a specific argument under T5, so tests fits.

tranche.reason: A specific theoretical argument that the per-layer superposition account (V3's mechanism) can't be a complete theory of feature representation if feature universality holds. That means a version needs restating. It has no measurements.

source_check.notes: Four-page theoretical note with no rows or experiments. It rests on Kaplan aspect-ratio invariance and on equal-loss models learning identical features. Its conclusion is a disjunction (superposition or universality needs revision), and it bears on V3 only indirectly: it is about the completeness of feature representation, not about what causes neuron polysemanticity. Table 1 is garbled in the text but can be recovered from the prose.
